explanation: Light takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, so radio talks with the Apollo astronauts had a pause of about 2.5 seconds between each question and its answer.

claims.text: In a vacuum, light travels 299,792,458 metres, about 300,000 km, in one second.
The average distance from Earth to the Moon is about 384,400 km.
Light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from Earth to the Moon.
A radio signal's round trip between Earth and the Moon takes about 2.5 seconds, which caused a noticeable pause in conversations with Apollo astronauts on the Moon.

writerNotes: Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3). lint: content:check run on the batch. claims: all listed; every claim holds a number, so all are high; c1 and c2 are the label claims of a counterintuitive item. datasets: no pinned dataset covers these; c1 is the SI definition of the metre (the speed of light is fixed at 299,792,458 m/s), c2 is the widely published mean distance, c3 is a calculation (384,400 / 299,792 is about 1.28 s) and c4 doubles it (about 2.56 s at the mean distance, about 2.4 s at perigee, so 'about 2.5' holds at that precision). No writer search spent. rivalTest: many players treat light as effectively instant and assume it would cross to the Moon within a second; the Moon is 1.28 times farther, which clears the 1.1 guard, and even at perigee (about 363,000 km) it is still farther than a light-second. Against the key: in air light is slower by a tiny fraction, which only widens the gap. volatility: evergreen. regional: no local knowledge. style: Oxford spelling, labels in the same noun-phrase form and under 40 characters, explanation 30 words. myths: screened; no hit expected. mystery and encore: not applicable. doubts: c4 depends on the Moon's distance on the day, so I kept 'about 2.5 seconds'.
